notes.meaning: Jesus warns that things leading people into sin will certainly happen in this fallen world, but the person who causes them faces severe judgment. A stumbling block describes a snare or temptation that trips someone up. Jesus says it would be better to drown with a heavy millstone tied around one's neck than to lead one of His vulnerable followers into sin.

Jesus tells His disciples to keep a close eye on their own hearts and actions. When a fellow believer sins, we must speak to them directly and honestly in love rather than holding a grudge. Whenever that person repents, even repeatedly within the same day, we are commanded to forgive them completely.

Realizing how hard it is to forgive someone again and again, the apostles ask Jesus to strengthen their faith. Jesus explains that the power does not come from having a massive amount of faith, but from the God in whom that faith rests. Even faith as tiny as a mustard seed can accomplish humanly impossible things, like uprooting a deep-rooted mulberry tree.

Jesus tells a story about a master and his servant to teach true humility. A servant who comes home from a hard day in the field still prepares the master's meal, because he is simply doing the work required of him. In the same way, believers should never think that obeying God earns special credit or puts Him in our debt, because doing His will is our basic duty as His servants.

differ.view: Good works can never place God in our debt or earn any merit, because even complete obedience is only what God already requires by right.
While humans cannot profit God by their work, God by His grace promises to reward obedience eternally.

notes.meaning: On His way to Jerusalem, Jesus travels along the border between Galilee and Samaria and meets ten men suffering from leprosy. Because the law required lepers to stay away from others to prevent spreading the disease, they shout from a distance for mercy. Jesus tells them to go present themselves to the priests for inspection, and as they step out in obedience and faith, their skin is completely healed.

When one of the men realizes he has been healed, he immediately turns around and praises God with a loud voice. He falls facedown at Jesus' feet to thank Him personally, and Luke notes that this grateful man is a Samaritan. This detail stands out because Jews and Samaritans usually avoided each other with deep suspicion.

Jesus asks why only one out of the ten returned to give glory to God, pointing out that this foreigner was the only one to show gratitude. He then tells the man to stand up and go, explaining that his faith had made him whole. While all ten men received physical healing in their bodies, this Samaritan also received a greater spiritual blessing through his trust in Christ.

When the Pharisees ask when God's kingdom will arrive, Jesus answers that it does not come with flashy outward pageantry that people can track like an earthly empire. They will not be able to point to a royal palace or an army and say it is confined there. Instead, the kingdom is already present in their midst because the King Himself is standing right before them.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some read this verse as meaning that the kingdom of God is an inner divine spark or spiritual potential hidden within every human being.

notes.meaning: Turning to His disciples, Jesus warns that difficult days are coming when they will deeply miss His physical presence and long for His return. He tells them not to run off chasing rumors of secret Messiah sightings, because His second coming will be as unmistakable and sudden as lightning flashing across the entire sky. But before that glorious day arrives, Jesus must first suffer rejection and death on the cross.

Jesus compares His future coming to the ancient days of Noah and Lot. In both stories, people went about their daily routines of eating, drinking, buying, and building, completely ignoring God's warnings until sudden judgment wiped them out. The danger Jesus highlights is spiritual indifference and false security, which leaves people totally unprepared for the day the Son of Man is revealed.

When that crisis arrives, no one should waste time running back inside a house or leaving a field to grab personal belongings. Jesus warns His followers to remember Lot's wife, who looked back longingly at Sodom and perished. Anyone who clings to earthly comforts to protect their physical life will lose what matters most, but those ready to surrender everything for Christ will preserve true life.

Jesus explains that His coming will bring a sudden and sharp separation between people who look identical on the outside. Two people sleeping in the same bed or two women grinding grain at the same millstone will be divided, with one taken and the other left behind. External closeness in work or home life cannot substitute for personal readiness before God.

differ.view: The one taken is snatched up in the rapture to meet Christ in the air, while the other is left behind to face the tribulation on earth.
The one taken is swept away in sudden judgment, just as sinners were taken away in the flood of Noah, while the one left is preserved for safety.

notes.meaning: The disciples ask where these dramatic events and separations will happen. Jesus replies with a common proverb, saying that wherever there is a dead body, vultures or birds of prey will quickly gather. This means that divine judgment will strike with certainty wherever spiritual death and moral corruption are found.
